qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: An overseas territory prints its own stamps, elects a local assembly, and runs its own schools — but the parent country's parliament controls its defense and foreign treaties and can veto any law the assembly passes. Which statement uses "sovereignty" accurately?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: The territory has full sovereignty, since it manages its own schools, stamps, and elections.
The territory has sovereignty over stamps but not treaties, so it is "partially sovereign" — the word is simply a matter of degree.
Sovereignty applies only to kingdoms ruled by a monarch, so the word cannot describe this territory either way.
The territory lacks sovereignty — a power above it can still veto and cancel any law it passes — so what it truly has is autonomy.

qti-content-body.p: Exactly. Sovereignty is supreme power that answers to nothing above it. Because the parent parliament controls defense and can strike down any law the assembly passes, the territory governs many of its own affairs — that is autonomy — without holding the final, top-of-the-chain power sovereignty names.

Sovereignty means supreme power with nothing above it, so it is all-or-nothing: running schools, stamps, and elections under a parliament that can strike down any law is self-government within limits — autonomy. The word is not a matter of degree, and it is not restricted to monarchies either.
